title: Dialects & Registers
keyIdea: English comes in many varieties. A dialect is the English of a place or group, with its own words and grammar: wee and bairn in Scotland, nowt in Yorkshire, y'all in the southern USA. Dialects follow regular rules, so they are not mistakes. Register is how formal you are for the listener and the moment. Writers use dialect, old forms and register in speech to show where and when a story is set and who a character is.

kid: There is more than one kind of English. A dialect is the English of a place or a group. In Scotland a small child can be a wee bairn. In Yorkshire, nowt means nothing. In the southern USA, y'all means all of you.

Dialects have rules, not just words. Some people say we was and you was. They use was with every person, every time. That is a pattern. Standard English says we were, and it is the variety we use in formal writing.
Register is how formal you are. Most people switch. Kirsty speaks Scots with her gran, chats with a friend, and says Yes, Mr Shah to a new teacher. Each one fits the listener.
Authors use this on purpose. A line in dialect shows where a character is from. Old words like thou and whither show a story set long ago. Posh or stiff words show what kind of person is talking.
adult: This topic is for ages 10 to 11. It matches the standard on comparing kinds of English in stories, plays and poems. Learners spot dialect words and dialect grammar. They tell dialect apart from register. They explain what a writer gains by putting speech in dialect or in older English.

Linguists treat a dialect as a full variety with steady grammar. We was, I done it and she don't are common in British and American dialects, and each follows a regular pattern. Standard English is also a dialect. It is the one used in formal writing, exams and most books. Register is separate: anyone can be more or less formal in their own dialect.

Common mistakes: calling dialect bad or lazy English, and mixing up dialect (where you are from) with register (how formal the moment is). Children also think old words like thou come from a place, not a time. Many think a translated line keeps everything. Be careful to praise the switch, not to erase home speech. The goal is to choose the variety that fits.

In the lab your child matches five dialect words to their meanings. Next they sort dialect grammar from Standard English. They pick what Kirsty says to her gran, a London friend and a new teacher. They decide if a story line shows where, when or who. Last, they translate a Scots line and watch the voice bar drop.

familyTip: Collect family words. Ask grandparents or neighbours for words they grew up with that you do not use, like bairn, nowt or y'all, and what they mean. Then read a story aloud with a character who speaks in dialect and ask: what does this tell us about where they live?

practice.prompt: In a story set in Scotland, a mum says, "Mind the wee bairn." What does she mean?
choices: Watch the small child
Find the lost bear
Leave the wet bin
practice.hint: Wee is a Scots word for small. Bairn is a Scots word for a person.
practice.explain: Wee means small and bairn means child in Scots. Mind means look after or watch.

practice.prompt: A character says "we was" on page {n} and "they was" on page {m}. What does that show?
choices: Her dialect uses was with every person
The author keeps making mistakes
She changes her mind about grammar
practice.hint: Is it random, or the same every time?
practice.explain: Using was with we and they every time, on page {n} and page {m}, is a regular dialect pattern. Standard English would say we were and they were.

practice.prompt: Kirsty says "Aye, ah'm fair puggled" to her gran but "I am very tired" to her new teacher. What is she changing?
choices: Her variety and register, to fit the listener
Her meaning
Her name
practice.hint: Both lines mean the same thing. Who is she talking to?
practice.explain: The meaning stays the same: she is tired. She switches from Scots with family to formal Standard English for a teacher.

practice.prompt: A play set {n} years ago has a knight say, "Whither goest thou?" Why does the writer use these words?
choices: To show the story is set long ago
To show the knight is from Australia
Because old words are more correct
practice.hint: Thou and whither are not from a place. They are from a time.
practice.explain: Thou and whither are old forms of English. They tell you the play is set in the past, about {n} years ago, not in a place today.

practice.prompt: You are writing a formal letter to the council. Which sentence fits best?
choices: We were told the park would open in May.
We was told the park would open in May.
Y'all told us the park would open in May.
practice.hint: Formal writing usually expects Standard English.
practice.explain: We were is the Standard English form, which suits a formal letter. We was and y'all are fine in speech and stories but do not fit this register.

choices: The English of a place or group, with its own words and grammar
English full of spelling mistakes
A language that is not English
pool.hint: Think of wee, nowt and y'all.
pool.explain: A dialect is a variety of English linked to a place or group. It has its own words and its own regular grammar.

pool.prompt: In Yorkshire dialect, "There's nowt in the fridge, and I've looked {n} times" means…
choices: There is nothing in the fridge
There is a lot in the fridge
The fridge is new
pool.hint: Nowt is the opposite of owt, which means anything.
pool.explain: Nowt means nothing in Yorkshire and other northern English dialects. Looking {n} times found nothing at all.

pool.prompt: What is the difference between dialect and register?
choices: Dialect is where you are from; register is how formal you are
They mean exactly the same
Register is only for writing; dialect is only for books
pool.hint: Kirsty keeps her home but changes how formal she is.
pool.explain: Dialect is linked to place or group. Register is how formal you are for the listener and the moment.

pool.prompt: An author writes a farm lad's speech as "tha mun come up on t' moor". What does the reader learn?
choices: Where the lad is from
That the author cannot spell
That the story is set in space
pool.hint: Tha, mun and t' are words from one part of England.
pool.explain: Tha, mun and t' are Yorkshire dialect, so the reader learns the lad is from the north of England.

pool.prompt: Ben uses dialect with friends and Standard English in a speech to {n} parents. What is true?
choices: He is choosing the variety that fits each audience
His dialect is wrong and he is fixing it
He should use the same words with everyone
pool.hint: Neither is wrong. Which fits a formal speech?
pool.explain: A speech to {n} parents is formal, so Standard English fits. Dialect fits friends. Switching is a skill.

pool.prompt: What happens when you translate a character's dialect into Standard English?
choices: The meaning stays, but the voice and sense of place are lost
Nothing changes
The meaning changes completely
pool.hint: Think of Kirsty's line after you swapped every Scots word.
pool.explain: The line becomes clear to any reader, but the character's voice and home are lost. That is why authors keep dialect.

choices: She doesn't like peas.
She don't like peas.
She dinnae like peas.
pool.hint: Standard English uses doesn't with she.
pool.explain: She doesn't is Standard English. She don't and she dinnae are dialect forms with their own rules.

pool.prompt: Why might a posh character say "One simply does not eat in the street"?
choices: The words show what kind of person she is
They show the story is set long ago
They show she is from Scotland
pool.hint: One simply is very formal and stiff.
pool.explain: One and simply mark a very formal, upper-class way of speaking, so they tell you who she is.

visual.caption: Is it about where, or about when? Drag each word, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match dialect words, sort dialect grammar, switch Kirsty's English for three listeners, read what dialogue tells you, translate a Scots line.
